core.text: 2 Preliminary & Problem Setup

We aim to develop a method that can help non-expert users steer strong LLMs and achieve professional results aligned with their true intent. Evaluating alignment is difficult because the human intention remains latent. In this section, we detail our research setup, which operationalizes the theoretical “sandwich” protocol to enable rigorous evaluation.
2.1 Preliminary: The “Sandwich" Protocol

Sandwiching experiments pose an empirical test of a scalable oversight technique’s ability to align a model (Bowman et al., 2022; Cotra, 2021). There are three roles: (1) The non-expert, who has intentions but is a weak supervisor. They cannot perform the task or oversee a model without assistance. (2) The model sandwiched between, which has sufficient capability to perform the task, but may not be aligned. (3) The expert, who has all the capabilities to reliably evaluate the output. The expert provides a good-faith evaluation signal without performing the task, serving as an approximate upper bound on achievable alignment under correct supervision. During the experiment, the non-expert uses a scalable oversight technique to supervise the model. The effect of the scalable oversight method can be measured by the gap in alignment achieved under non-expert supervision versus expert supervision.
2.2 Problem Setup

We consider a scalable oversight setting in which a non-expert user seeks to align a strong language model with their latent intent, despite being unable to fully specify or verify the desired outcome. We situate the problem in the context of vibe coding, where users express software requirements in natural language and the system autonomously produces development artifacts. Directly evaluating alignment at the level of a complete software system is costly and capability-intensive: reviewing large codebases requires substantial expertise and is easily confounded by code-level implementation issues rather than requirement misalignment. Instead, we adopt the Product Requirements Document (PRD) as an evaluation pivot: a PRD captures the requirements while being substantially easier to assess than the final implementation itself (Jackson, 2012; Wiegers and Beatty, 2013). Alignment is therefore evaluated by how well the PRD generated by the model reflects the user’s underlying intent. To enable rigorous evaluation, we instantiate the Sandwich Protocol under our setting:

The weak human (non-expert): The user ℋ\mathcal{H} cannot fully specify their intent or reliably verify execution outcomes due to limited cognitive bandwidth or insufficient software development expertise. As a result, ℋ\mathcal{H} can only provide an initial, high-level query qq, even though the user has an underlying intent ℐ\mathcal{I} that constitutes the target of alignment.

The model to supervise: The model generates a PRD 𝒟∗\mathcal{D}^{*} in response to the user’s query. While it is capable of producing a complete PRD, its output may deviate from the user’s true intent ℐ\mathcal{I} in the absence of effective supervision.

Expert evaluator. The expert does not participate in the generation process. Instead, the expert evaluates the degree of alignment between the final document 𝒟∗\mathcal{D}^{*} and the targeted user intent ℐ\mathcal{I}. Consistent with the Sandwich Protocol, this assessment serves as an approximate upper bound of correct supervision, considering the intent as the observable “golden standard".

Under this setup, our research objective is to develop scalable oversight methods that enable alignment achieved under weak human supervision to approach that achievable expert-level supervision. Concretely, we measure how closely the output 𝒟∗\mathcal{D}^{*} approaches the target intent ℐ\mathcal{I} according to expert evaluation, and treat this as an indicator of how effectively weak human supervision is amplified.
3 Method: Scalable Interactive Oversight
In this section, we introduce an interaction agent that provides scalable oversight throughout the interaction process. It works in a decomposition-interaction loop:

Given a natural language instruction qq by a human, the agent first decomposes the incoming long-horizon task into a tree-structured interaction plan 𝒯0\mathcal{T}^{0}. In the context of web-dev requirements, the leaf nodes correspond to concrete development modules (e.g., parent: UI design; child: display rule).

At this stage, the user provides supervision. For each leaf node vtv^{t}, the agent engages the user through low-burden queries tailored to the current subtask, and the user makes feedback based on the intentions (① in Figure 1). Specifically, we constrain the interaction questions in a closed form (primarily issues selection-based or ranking-based queries). Users may also respond with DontCare (outside their concern) or DontKnow (beyond their understanding), allowing the interaction to adapt.

After completing the interaction for a leaf node, the agent summarizes the elicited feedback into a compact node preference 𝒫t\mathcal{P}^{t} and adds it to a cumulative preference state (② in Figure 1). Then the agent updates the interaction plan conditioned on the cumulative preference state (𝒯t→𝒯(t+1)\mathcal{T}^{t}\rightarrow\mathcal{T}^{(t+1)}, ③ in Figure 1), allowing future interactions to be adaptively shaped by previously expressed user intent.

This loop continues until all nodes are visited. At termination, the interaction agent is considered to have fully accumulated the user’s preferences, producing a global preference state that can be input to downstream generation. Algorithm 1 formalizes this interaction. All of the prompts we used in the workflow are presented in Appendix C. We illustrate interaction cases in Appendix B.4.

Simplifying supervision. First, users are only required to provide selection or ranking feedback, rather than fully specifying requirements in natural language. Because comparative judgments impose lower cognitive demands than requirement specification (Radhakrishnan et al., 2023), this design makes supervision easier for users.

Amplifying supervision signal. The interaction agent recursively amplifies weak supervision signals by accumulating user preferences across the interaction tree. This is inspired by the previous scalable oversight methods (Christiano et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021). Through this recursive preference propagation, the human feedback can be transformed into increasingly strong supervision as interactions increase, enabling more effective alignment. Second, by decomposing a complex task into a tree of localized subtasks, the system relieves users from managing a large global scope. As a result, non-expert users can provide supervision without needing a holistic understanding of the entire scope.

Scaling interaction. The tree-based architecture inherently supports interactions of arbitrary depth, offering a scalable path toward aligning increasingly complex systems. As long as the user’s cognitive load permits, the tree can be expanded indefinitely to facilitate human-AI collaboration on increasingly sophisticated tasks.
4 Empirical Validation of Scalable Interactive Oversight Framework at Test Time
4.1 Setup

Task and Dataset. We focus on enabling non-expert users to produce professional website development requirements that align with their true intent. To operationalize this evaluation objective, we construct PRDs based on real-world websites and regard them as the true intent ℐ\mathcal{I} for the users. Specifically, we crawl production websites to collect their complete UI components, and use search-augmented LLM to gather additional publicly available information, such as related GitHub repositories and other functional descriptions. Using the detailed function description and UI components. Then we use LLMs to generate a structured PRD for each website, omitting low-level technical details to better reflect non-expert requirements. Following established practices in software engineering (Wiegers and Beatty, 2013), we structure all PRDs into five modules: product overview, core function, non-functional requirements, business rules, and user experience design. See PRD cases in Appendix B.3.

We then synthesize an initial user request qq (e.g., “I want to build a recipe-sharing platform”) that a non-expert might plausibly provide during vibe coding. The initial requirement tree 𝒯0\mathcal{T}^{0} is generated from qq with the five root nodes. We sample 37 test cases for the test time validation.

Following the “sandwich" setting in Section 2, we evaluate the similarity between the generated 𝒟∗\mathcal{D}^{*} and the target intent ℐ\mathcal{I} using a rubric-based evaluation. Each ℐ\mathcal{I} is decomposed into atomic requirements ℛ={r1,…,rm}\mathcal{R}=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}\} (e.g., “user authentication methods”, “responsive design”), and we compute the Alignment Score as follows:
Alignment Score​(𝒟∗)=1|ℛ|​∑ri∈ℛ𝕀⁡[ri​ satisfied in ​𝒟∗]\text{Alignment Score}(\mathcal{D}^{*})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r_{i}\in\mathcal{R}}\mathbb{I}[r_{i}\text{ satisfied in }\mathcal{D}^{*}]
In large scale evaluation, we applied LLM-judge based on Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct. We provide LLM-judge details and its validation in Appendix A.2.

To scale our experiments, we develop a user simulator ℋ⁡(ℐ,q)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{I},q) that emulates non-expert user behavior during interaction. Conditioned on the ground-truth intent ℐ\mathcal{I}, the initial query qq, and a non-expert role specification, the simulator interacts with the system and provides feedback throughout the workflow. We implement the simulator with deepseek-R1, chosen for its strong role-playing capability. We validate the simulation against a test set of real user interactions to ensure fidelity. More details about user simulation are in Appendix A.3.

We compare our method against two baselines: (1) Direct PRD generation with popular vibe coding framework without interaction, e.g., codex, claude-code, gemini-cli. (2) Vanilla interaction: vanilla multi-turn free-form dialogue to generate a PRD. We use GPT-5, claude-sonnet-4.5, and gemini2.5-pro as the PRD generator, i.e., the strong but maybe misaligned model under the “sandwich" setting. For the interaction model in vanilla interaction and ours, we use the corresponding model to interact with the users as well as the tree updating (except for the gemini experiment, because it doesn’t adhere well to JSON format tree structures, so we used o4-mini for tree structure updates. Results in Section 4.3 shows that this didn’t significantly affect the results). Details baseline settings are in Appendix A.1.
4.2 Results

Table 1 presents results on simulated users across PRD modules. Module-level scores are the fraction of satisfied rubrics per module, and the overall score is the fraction satisfied across all modules. Our method exhibit remarkable improvement over the baselines on the alignment metric. Both popular vibe coding frameworks and vanilla interaction struggle to capture nuanced user intent in comprehensive PRDs. On GPT-5, we achieves substantial improvements of 33% and 39% over vanilla interaction and codex, respectively. On claude-sonnet-4.5, we achieve 0.618 on average, consistently outperforming both vanilla interaction and claude code. Notably, the improvement is also pronounced on Gemini-2.5-pro: our framework increases the average score from 0.359 (vanilla interaction) to 0.554, corresponding to a +54% relative gain.

Across modules, the largest and most consistent gains appear on Module 2 (core function), which most directly reflects users’ core needs (e.g., +0.24 on GPT-5 vs. codex, +0.15 on gemini-2.5-pro over vanilla interaction). Modules 3–5 generally exhibit lower across methods, likely because user intent is harder to infer at these stages. Our approach mitigates this difficulty and improves late-stage performance, achieving up to +0.21 on Module 5. Overall, Ours improves average performance while demonstrating sustained alignment as interaction progresses and preferences accumulate.

The tree-structured decomposition provides scalability for our framework. To evaluate whether scaling interaction boosts the performance, we generate an intermediate PRD based on the accumulated preferences and evaluate its alignment with the oriented one every 5 interaction nodes. Figure 3(left) illustrates the alignment score evolution on GPT-5. The improvement in alignment with the increasing number of interaction nodes indicates that our method has good scalability in future applications.

From requirement documents generated by the no-interaction baseline and our method, we generate corresponding full-stack websites using claude-opus-4.5 under the claude code framework, and evaluate their alignment with the same evaluation method. We evaluate the alignment of the resulting implementations using the same rubric-based evaluation as in the PRD-level assessment, with claude-opus-4.5 acting as the LLM judge under the claude code framework as well. We additionally ask human judges to score successfully deployable implementations. The results are reported in Table 2. Our method consistently outperforms the baseline under both LLM-based and human evaluation, indicating improved alignment. We show some examples of the deployed website in Appendix B.2.

Partial execution traces of our framework are shown in Figure 4 (see Appendix B.4 for detailed examples). The cases indicate the three fact: (1) User preferences directly dictate the dynamic reconfiguration of the tree structure; (2) When facing the ambiguous or uncertain user inputs the system proactively initiates clarification cycles and adjusts the interaction strategy to ensure data integrity; (3) When aligning users, the system ensures that the proposed options meet the requirements of advancement.
4.3 Ablation Study
Using the vanilla multi-turn interaction as a baseline, we analyze the incremental impact of our proposed components on the first two modules(Figure 3):

Easy supervision: We first evaluate the effect of providing interaction policy that ease the feedback by removing the tree-based preference propagation. The results show moderate gains (e.g., a 4.7% improvement in Module 2), indicating that constraining user feedback into closed formats helps reliable feedback.

Tree-based preference propagation: To isolate the system effects from model capacity, we replace the full controller with a lightweight model (o4-mini) for tree updates. Even this lightweight variant yields a substantial gain (e.g., +11.7% on Module 2), indicating that explicit interaction state management and preference propagation play an important role beyond controller model scaling.
4.4 Real-user Study on Alignment Effectiveness

We hired a non-expert to engage in our interaction system. The user is required to collaborate with the GPT-5 based on the given requirements, to generate professional-level documents. Due to the resource limit, we conduct the experiments on 10 cases. The results also indicate the trend: The more interaction, the more aligned. For every three interaction nodes, we use the accumulated preference to generate the document with GPT-5. The results is illustrated in Figure 3(right), exhibiting the increase in alignment scores as interaction rounds progress. And the user reported that: It enables detailed and in-depth control. There are detailed real-user interaction cases in Appendix B.1.
5 Training Interactive Agents with RL from Online Human Feedback

Although RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022) is a common technique for improving model alignment, it still relies on comparing or rating outputs (Wang et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). In software development tasks, this is hard for non-expert users. In this section, we validate that we can directly use online feedback signals from weak supervisors to optimize the interaction agent. An external evaluator could further provide effective reward signals.
5.1 Reinforcement Learning Setup & Formalization

Given query qjq_{j}, at node v1v_{1}, the policy πinteraction\pi_{\text{interaction}} interacts with simulated user ℋ⁡(ℐj,qj)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{I}_{j},q_{j}) to produce Sj,1S_{j,1}. Then πinteraction\pi_{\text{interaction}} updates ℳ\mathcal{M} with node preference, select next node, obtain Sj,2S_{j,2}. Iterate until all nodes are resolved to yield PRD Dj∗D_{j}^{*}. Because traces are multi-turn and do not share prefixes, each input typically produces multiple training sequences (see Figure 5, left).

We trained a Qwen3-30B-A3B model as the initial policy. We use gemini-2.5-pro as the doc generator and use o4-mini to update the requirement tree for the rollout. For the advantage calculating, we use a variant to GRPO algorithm (Shao et al., 2024). Detailed training settings and parameter comparison experiments are presented in Appendix A.4.
5.2 Online Reward from Weak-supervisor

We first focus on whether we can rely entirely on weak supervision signals from users to align the model. Therefore, we design a User Reward (UR): for each trainable interaction sequence Sj,iS_{j,i}, we count the proportion of DontCare responses from the user as a penalty reward. Formally:
U​R​(Sj,i)=−∑t=1|Sj,i|𝕀[ft=DontCare]|Sj,i|UR(S_{j,i})=-\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{|S_{j,i}|}\mathbb{I}[f^{t}=\texttt{DontCare}]}{|S_{j,i}|}

This reward encourages the model to minimize the frequency of DontCare responses, thereby promoting more effective and engaging interactions that better capture user intent. Notably, this reward is purely online.

The interaction could be optimized with the signal from the non-expert user only, as Figure 6(left) shows. With the training reward increase over steps, which means the ratio that the user expresses DontCare decreases, the alignment score also increases. This result is exciting because it demonstrates a weak-to-strong optimization effect, where non-experts’ feedback at interaction time is sufficient to guide stronger models. From another perspective, this makes online training possible because the reward is online.
5.3 Combining Reward from Expert Evaluator

Further, we incorporate an Expert Reward based on the evaluation of generated PRDs. A direct reward is Outcome Reward (OR), using the alignment score between generated PRD Dj∗D_{j}^{*} and oriented intent ℐ\mathcal{I}. Each Sj,_S_{j,\_} could share the same outcome reward. Considering the scarcity of final reward, we also design Progressive Reward(PR) to evaluate node-level interaction gain. At each node viv^{i}, there is accumulated preference conclusions 𝒫j1,…,𝒫ji−1{\mathcal{P}^{1}_{j},\ldots,\mathcal{P}^{i-1}_{j}} and a new conclusion 𝒫ji\mathcal{P}^{i}_{j}. The P​Rj,iPR_{j,i} evaluates whether the existence of 𝒫ji\mathcal{P}^{i}_{j} could make progress in the alignment between accumulated preferences and the oriented ℐj\mathcal{I}_{j}. The llm judge prompt of the progressive reward is presented in Appendix C.7. In optimization, we use the reward as their combination for the jt​hj_{th} sample in the batch:
R⁡(Sj)=∑i(P​Rj,i+U​Rj,i)/n+0.5∗O​RjR(S_{j})=\sum^{i}({PR_{j,i}+UR_{j,i}})/n+0.5*OR_{j}

The combination of the reward from both the user and expert further enhances the optimization as the Figure 6 shows. This reward makes the system achieve a higher alignment score. However, the online reward makes the training dynamic stabler. In Appendix A.4, we present the ablation study of the reward design, which indicates that all of the rewards could boost the RL training.

5.4 RL Enhances Generalization and Efficiency

Both reward designs exhibit generalization to untrained modules and unseen test settings. The RL training is conducted within Module 1 and Module 2. During the test time, we use the best-performance models to conduct full interaction both under the RL training settings and GPT-5 setting. The results are shown in Table 3, although M3–M5 are not included during RL training, both “User Reward" and “User+Expert Reward" setting show improved performance on these untrained modules. Under the same-as-training setting, “User+Expert Reward" improves the average score on M3–M5 from 0.500 to 0.518. This trend is further amplified under the GPT-5 setting, where the average score on the untrained module increases from 0.606 to 0.640.

We visualize the change in the number of interaction nodes over the course of RL training in Figure 7. No matter whether measured by the total number of interaction rounds (left) or the number of interaction rounds per node (right), both metrics exhibit a clear downward trend, indicating that RL training enables the model to conduct more effective interactions and acquire information with higher efficiency.
6 Related Work

Scalable oversight. Superalignment emphasizes the need to steer and control AI systems that are much more capable than humans (OpenAI, 2023). Scalable oversight addresses this challenge by reframing supervision as an easier task, enabling humans to oversee models beyond their direct capabilities. Prior work has explored several scalable oversight paradigms, including AI critique (Saunders et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2022; Xi et al., 2024; McAleese et al., 2024), where auxiliary models evaluate or verify outputs; amplification, which decomposes complex tasks into simpler subproblems (Christiano et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021); and debate, which surfaces errors and misalignment by eliciting competing arguments for human judgment (Irving et al., 2018). ‘Sandwiching’ framework is proposed to measure the effectiveness of an alignment method (Cotra, 2021; Bowman et al., 2022). However, most of these paradigms primarily focus on evaluating, decomposing, or contesting model outputs, rather than shaping user intent before execution. We bridge this gap by implementing a practical interactive framework that enables non-experts to effectively align AI agents.

The rapid evolution of large language models has transformed the role of AI in software engineering from a passive code-writing aid into an active, agentic collaborator (OpenAI, 2025; Anthropic, 2025; Google, 2025). This transformation has introduced an emergent development approach - often referred to as Vibe Coding- in which programmers rely on behavioral validation of AI-produced systems, emphasizing empirical outcomes over direct examination of the underlying source code (Karpathy, 2025; Horvat, 2025; Ge et al., 2025; Ray, 2025). However, this new paradigm presents reliability challenges. Quantitative research shows that collaborating with code agents unexpectedly increases the task-completion time for 19% (Becker et al., 2025). The limitation of natural language in expressing complex development requirements has exposed (Treude and Gerosa, 2025; Schmidt et al., 2024).
